services.justification: Runs 20261010-171948-pod_kill-cartservice, 20261010-183547-pod_kill-cartservice, and 20261010-173035-memory_stress-cartservice show 83–100% peak errors, broad flow impact, and up to 42 s recovery. The service is a single-replica dependency of all flows.

Runs 20261010-101701-pod_kill-productcatalogservice and 20261010-171613-network_delay-productcatalogservice show broad errors and roughly 700 ms p95 on multiple flows under catalog delay; pod-kill runs also report 5 s p95 and about 21–24 s recovery. Its single-replica, all-flow reach and observed recommendationservice NotReady event lower containment.

Runs 20261010-172943-pod_failure-redis-cart and 20261010-185925-pod_failure-redis-cart recorded frontend unresponsiveness, roughly 5000 ms p95, and high peak error rates before abort. Its one stateful replica holds cart data and is shared across the shopping path.

Runs 20261010-194328-network_loss-currencyservice and 20261010-203618-pod_failure-currencyservice show p95 of 3153.7 ms under 20% loss and 50% impact error rate during pod failure across four flows. Recovery was relatively quick, but the shared single replica has broad flow reach.

Runs 20261010-080822-traffic_spike-frontend and 20261010-202852-traffic_spike-frontend measured p95 of 4170 ms and 1664.6 ms, respectively, with frontend CPU at or near its 200m limit and severe throttling. Reported request error rates stayed at zero, but every flow slowed and the entrypoint is a single replica.

Runs 20261010-170944-pod_failure-paymentservice and 20261010-203207-pod_failure-paymentservice show 83–90% checkout errors while the other measured flows remained error-free. The impact is severe for checkout but confined to that flow, and the single replica limits posture.

Run 20261010-203716-network_delay-recommendationservice had zero errors but p95 factors of 7.36x on product, 6.55x on view_cart, and 5.38x on checkout; its pod-kill run reported no flow errors. It remains a single replica, and observed latency affects several dependent flows.

Run 20261010-173902-network_delay-shippingservice showed checkout p95 141.0 ms and view_cart p95 55.0 ms with no errors; 20261010-190144-pod_kill-shippingservice measured no errors, though it sampled zero checkout or view_cart requests. Evidence supports a latency sensitivity, not a demonstrated outage.

In 20261010-074206-pod_kill-adservice, no flow errors were measured and home p95 was 19.5 ms versus a 12.5 ms run baseline; other flows were near baseline. The single replica limits posture despite the measured containment.

In 20261010-173821-pod_kill-checkoutservice and 20261010-190036-memory_stress-checkoutservice, no errors or material measured slowdown were reported. The kill run sampled zero checkout requests, so checkout availability during the kill is not demonstrated; posture remains limited by one replica.

In 20261010-173649-pod_failure-emailservice, all sampled flows had zero errors and checkout p95 was 19.4 ms; the run reported no affected flows. The single replica is a static weakness, but no user impact was measured.

ai.summary: Experiments reveal significant weaknesses in the shared cart and catalog paths, where a single service failure can disrupt multiple shopping flows and recovery may take tens of seconds. Traffic spikes also expose frontend CPU throttling: p95 latency reached several seconds while the frontend was throttled at nearly 100%. Currency and payment failures impaired checkout or other dependent flows, while the tested ad, email, and shipping failures showed little or no measured user impact. These findings are based on short experiments with small per-flow samples, so the observed impact is evidence of risk rather than a precise production failure-rate estimate.

findings.title: Cartservice pod loss disrupts every shopping flow and recovery is slow
findings.evidence: Across these pod-kill runs, all five flows were affected; peak error rate was 100%, with impact error rates of 90.08%, 83.33%, and 92.66%. In the latter two runs the replacement pod became ready in 23.1–23.2 s and user-facing recovery took 28.2–31.2 s. The service has one replica and is shared by frontend and checkoutservice.
findings.root_cause: Cartservice is a single-replica shared dependency. When its pod is killed, there is no serving replica during replacement, so requests across dependent flows fail or wait until the new pod becomes ready.
findings.fix_rationale: Cartservice is stateless in the dependency map, so a second replica can continue serving while Kubernetes replaces a failed pod and reduce the single-pod outage.
findings.expected_improvement: During a repeat pod kill, requests should continue through the surviving replica, reducing the broad error burst and avoiding a roughly 23-second wait for replacement before service is available again.

findings.title: Redis-cart unavailability stalls cart-dependent requests instead of failing fast
findings.evidence: Redis pod-failure runs were aborted after frontend unresponsiveness of 4.2–4.6 s; peak p95 reached 5003.7 and 5002.5 ms, with peak error rates of 66.7% and 100%. The first run observed only the home flow before the abort, so its other flows were not adequately sampled. Separately, 20% packet loss on cartservice was aborted at p95 1571.4 ms; add_to_cart reached 1378.0 ms and view_cart 1480.9 ms.
findings.root_cause: The cart request path synchronously depends on the single stateful Redis service. The long request stalls under Redis unavailability and high cartservice packet loss indicate insufficiently bounded waits and isolation for cart operations.

fix.change: Set a 200 ms deadline on cartservice-to-redis-cart calls and return a typed cart-unavailable result on timeout. Make frontend handlers avoid blocking home and product rendering on optional cart reads; fail cart mutations and checkout explicitly rather than waiting for the request timeout.

findings.fix_rationale: Bounded calls limit how long Redis faults can hold requests open, and separating optional cart display from core page rendering can contain cart-backend failure without pretending cart mutations succeeded.
findings.expected_improvement: Redis failure or cartservice packet loss should no longer leave frontend requests stalled for several seconds; cart-dependent operations may still be unavailable, but unrelated page rendering should remain responsive and affected requests should fail promptly.

findings.title: Product catalog pod loss causes broad errors, long tail latency, and observed blast radius beyond the target
findings.evidence: The first pod-kill run recorded 100% peak error rate, peak p95 5003.9 ms, and recovery in 21.1 s; the guard reported frontend unresponsive for 3.2 s and a non-target recommendationservice pod NotReady. Another kill reached 5002.9 ms p95 and recovery in 23.6 s, with a recommendationservice pod also reported NotReady. The fallback pod-failure run aborted at 60% error rate, with impact error rate 59.09%.
findings.root_cause: Productcatalogservice is a single-replica dependency with reach across all flows and callers including frontend, checkoutservice, and recommendationservice. Losing its only pod causes dependent calls to fail or wait for timeouts while Kubernetes replaces it; the observed NotReady recommendation pod indicates potential blast-radius spillover.
findings.fix_rationale: The service is stateless in the dependency map. A second replica can maintain catalog availability while a failed pod is replaced and reduce reliance on a single pod for every flow.
findings.expected_improvement: A repeat pod kill should produce fewer catalog-related request failures and less multi-flow interruption; monitor recommendationservice readiness as well as catalog and frontend responses.

findings.title: Memory pressure can restart cartservice and make most shopping requests fail
findings.evidence: A 110 MB allocation against cartservice's 128 MiB memory limit produced a 97.19% impact error rate, peak error rate 100%, errors across all five flows, one cartservice restart, and 42 s recovery. The worst-flow p95 was 634.0 ms; the run was aborted after the error-rate guard fired.
findings.root_cause: The single cartservice container has little memory headroom for the tested allocation. Memory stress caused a restart and disrupted the shared cart path, so failures propagated across flows that depend on cartservice.
findings.fix_rationale: Increasing the memory limit provides more headroom for allocation spikes and reduces the likelihood that memory pressure will restart the only cartservice pod. The CPU limit is also raised as a concrete resource adjustment, although the cited run chiefly demonstrates memory-related impact.
findings.expected_improvement: The same 110 MB stress should be less likely to restart cartservice; if requests remain healthy, broad errors and the 42-second recovery interval should be avoided.

findings.title: Frontend CPU throttling makes all flows extremely slow under traffic spikes
findings.evidence: At 100 users, all flows were affected and peak p95 was 999.9 ms; frontend CPU peaked at 97.6% of its 200m limit with 96.6% peak throttling. At 500 users, all flows were affected and peak p95 reached 4170.0 ms; frontend CPU reached its 200m limit with 100% throttling. A 300-user run was aborted after p95 crossed 1500 ms.
findings.root_cause: Every request passes through the single frontend replica, whose 200m CPU limit is saturated and heavily throttled under load. That entrypoint bottleneck raises latency across all flows even though the VM-level CPU peaks reported in the runs were substantially lower.
findings.fix_rationale: The measured bottleneck is CPU throttling at the frontend's 200m limit, while measured memory use remained below the 128 MiB limit. Raising the CPU limit directly addresses that quota bottleneck; the single-node environment still limits the total capacity available.
findings.expected_improvement: At the same traffic levels, frontend throttling should fall and the multi-second p95 tail should improve. The rerun should establish whether node capacity, rather than the container limit, becomes the next bottleneck.

findings.title: Currencyservice delay, loss, and failure propagate to core flows
findings.evidence: With 50 ms added latency, home p95 was 521.3 ms and checkout p95 168.8 ms. At 5% packet loss, checkout p95 was 219.6 ms; at 20% loss, product p95 reached 3153.7 ms and the run was aborted. During pod failure, peak error rate was 80%, impact error rate 50%, and home, product, view_cart, and checkout were affected.
findings.root_cause: Currencyservice is a single-replica dependency shared by frontend and checkoutservice. Slow or unavailable currency RPCs propagate into several flows; under higher packet loss, the observed tail latency suggests callers wait too long for responses.

fix.change: Set a 200 ms end-to-end deadline on frontend and checkoutservice gRPC calls to currencyservice, and do not retry after the deadline. Return an explicit conversion-unavailable result rather than holding the user request open.

findings.fix_rationale: A bounded deadline limits latency propagation during slow or lossy calls, and avoiding retries prevents the configured caller behavior from extending the wait. This bounds waiting; it does not make a required currency conversion succeed when the service is unavailable.
findings.expected_improvement: Currency-related tails should be bounded below the several-second range seen at 20% packet loss. Requests that require conversion may still return an explicit error during an outage, but should not remain stalled for an extended timeout.

findings.title: Paymentservice failure breaks most checkout requests
findings.evidence: Checkout error rates were 83.3%, 75%, and 90% in these runs, while non-checkout flows reported zero errors. Peak aggregate error rate reached 21% in the first and third runs; the third run recorded 6 s recovery. Paymentservice has one replica and is on the checkout path.
findings.root_cause: The sole paymentservice replica is required by checkoutservice. When it is unavailable, most sampled checkout requests fail; the narrow impact is contained to checkout rather than spreading to the other observed flows.
findings.fix_rationale: Paymentservice is stateless in the dependency map, so a second replica can maintain payment capacity during a single-pod failure and reduce the checkout interruption.
findings.expected_improvement: A repeat pod-failure test should show fewer failed checkout requests while the affected pod is replaced; other flows should remain unaffected as in the evidence runs.

findings.title: Productcatalogservice latency is amplified across dependent flows
findings.evidence: With 100 ms added catalog latency, repeated runs measured product p95 around 711–715 ms, view_cart around 712–713 ms, checkout around 717–732 ms, and add_to_cart around 104–105 ms, with no measured errors. A 500 ms delay run was aborted; product p95 reached 1612.6 ms and overall peak p95 was 1368.3 ms.
findings.root_cause: Productcatalogservice is called by several services and reaches every flow. The large end-to-end increase from a 100 ms injected delay is consistent with latency amplification through dependent calls without sufficiently tight call deadlines.

fix.change: Set a 250 ms gRPC deadline for productcatalogservice calls in frontend, recommendationservice, and checkoutservice call sites. For optional recommendation data, return without recommendations on timeout; fail required catalog or checkout work promptly rather than waiting through an unbounded call.

findings.fix_rationale: Deadlines cap how long a slow catalog call can hold dependent requests open, while graceful fallback for optional recommendation data avoids turning an optional feature into a blocking dependency.
findings.expected_improvement: The same 100 ms injected delay should produce a substantially lower end-to-end p95 than the measured roughly 700 ms on several flows. Calls that exceed the deadline may fail promptly, so error rates and successful-response rates must be checked alongside latency.

ai.score_explanation: Scores start from the supplied anchors and remain within 15 points of each anchor. Higher criticality weights go to the entrypoint and checkout/cart path; optional advertising, recommendations, and email receive lower weights. The anchors already encode measured flow impact, so scores remain close to them except where a specific result warrants a bounded adjustment, such as the very small checkoutservice kill sample, the checkout-only scope of payment failure, and the observed recommendationservice NotReady spillover during catalog pod kills. All services have measured experiments in the supplied anchors table; posture scores remain at the anchored 60 because each listed deployment has one replica despite probes and limits.
ai.planner_review: Planner predictions were strong for several high-impact tests: productcatalogservice pod failure, productcatalogservice 100 ms delay, cartservice 110 MB memory stress, currencyservice pod failure, and recommendationservice 30 ms delay were marked confirmed. The planner correctly anticipated broad cart and Redis impact, but the Redis prediction for the first run overstated the observed flow coverage; early guard aborts and very small samples make that mismatch hard to interpret. Predictions were refuted for shippingservice memory stress, checkoutservice pod kill, and productcatalogservice memory stress at 110–112 MB; later 124 MB product-catalog stress did trigger errors, illustrating the importance of dose. Some partial misses also concern effect-size or flow scope: currencyservice 5% loss caused severe checkout latency without errors, and the checkoutservice kill sampled no checkout requests, so its apparent lack of impact is not a strong prediction validation.
limitations: The system runs on a single-node Kubernetes environment, so these runs do not test node failure, multi-node placement, or real cluster-level redundancy.

Many flow-level samples are small (often 4–24 requests), especially in aborted pod-failure and pod-kill runs; zero observed errors or absent flow measurements should not be treated as proof of resilience.
Experiments are short, and safety guards truncate some of the most severe network, resource, and pod-failure tests; long-duration degradation and repeated-failure behavior remain uncertain.

Traffic tests share one VM with the application and load generator. The reported VM CPU stayed substantially below 100%, but single-node resource contention still limits extrapolation to production capacity.
Run baselines and flow sample counts vary across experiments, so comparisons use the supplied run-specific measurements and should not be interpreted as a controlled long-term benchmark.
